To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) echolocation calls of twenty species of southern African bats, obtained with time-expansion detectors, were analysed, (b) call parameters and sonograms of eight species have not been previously reported, (c) echolocation calls from room-flown or hand-held bats matched, reasonably closely with those obtained from natural flying individuals, (d) call parameters and species identification were useful for identifying species of unknown call sequences, and (e) intraspecific variation of call parameters and species-specific

(1) the echolocation calls of 20 southern African bat species were recorded, and (2) the recordings were analysed to assess intraspecific and interspecific variability in call parameters and to determine whether echolocation calls of room-flown or hand-held individuals are similar to those of free-flying individuals.

(1) time expansion bat detectors provide reliable echolocation data on southern African bat species; (2) echolocation call structure is species-specific, but there is some intraspecific variability; (3) echolocation calls from naturally flying bats match those from room-flown and hand-held bats; (4) recordings from room-flowns and hand-held bats can be used to identify unknown call sequences from bats in natural habitats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a methodology for identifying species from their echolocation calls.

the development of an echolocation call library for southern African bat species, and with the potential use of this information for the identification of bat species from call sequences recorded with the Pettersson 0980 time expansion bat detector, or from call sequences recorded in other situations with time expansion or heterodyne bat-detectors.
the use of echolocation calls for species identification and the development of a database of southern African bat echolocation calls.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, time-expansion recordings of echolocation calls from room-flown or hand-held bats are useful, but should be used with care and in conjunction with other data.
time-expansion bat detectors are useful, but that the data they yield should always be considered cautiously, and in the context of other available information.

the echolocation calls of most species can be identified, with a high degree of certainty, using a time expansion detector, but that the echolocation call of a few species can only be identified with certainty by the use of additional information, such as the harmonic structure of the echolocation call, the flight behaviour and/or the presence of the species in the area at the time of the recording.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the absence of direct visual observations or other evidence, the use of a time-expansion detector and the measurement of dominant frequency and harmonic content, together with a consideration of the overall echolocation call structure, can provide a useful, although imperfect, means of species identification in the field.
time expansion detectors are the most useful tools available at present for the identification of echolocating bat species in southern Africa.
time-expansion detectors are useful for the identification of southern African bat species in general, and for the identification of unknown species in particular.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of time expansion bat detectors in the field, and in the laboratory (in a room), is a valuable tool to obtain echolocation call data, which can be used for species identification and for the study of echolocation in bats.
, in general, echolocation calls of bats can be reliably identified by species, using time-expanded bat detector recordings.
, with a few caveats, time-expansion recordings can be used to accurately identify bat species in southern Africa.
